claim: Basal cells are multipotent stem cells of a variety of organs, including the respiratory tract.
source: Basal cells are multipotent stem cells of a variety of organs, including the respiratory tract, where they are major components of the airway epithelium.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that references established scientific knowledge about basal cells.

claim: Six distinct basal cell subpopulations were identified in the adult murine trachea using single cell RNA-sequencing.
source: Using single cell RNA-sequencing and functional approaches, we report a significant and previously underappreciated degree of heterogeneity in the basal cell pool, leading to identification of six subpopulations in the adult murine trachea.
evidence: The manuscript describes scRNA-Seq experiments that identified six BC subpopulations, with data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Two major basal cell subpopulations collectively comprise the most uncommitted of all the basal cell pools.
source: Among these, we found two major subpopulations, collectively comprising the most uncommitted of all the pools, but with distinct gene expression signatures.
evidence: This is based on scRNA-Seq analysis showing BC-1 and BC-2 lack enrichment in differentiation markers compared to other BC subpopulations.

claim: The two major basal cell subpopulations occupy distinct ventral and dorsal tracheal niches.
source: Notably, these occupy distinct ventral and dorsal tracheal niches and differ in their ability to self-renew and initiate a program of differentiation in response to environmental perturbations in primary cultures and in mouse injury models in vivo.
evidence: Immunofluorescence data in Figure 2 shows differential spatial distribution of BC-1 and BC-2 markers in ventral and dorsal trachea.

claim: Basal cell heterogeneity is acquired prenatally when the basal cell pool and local niches are still being established.
source: We found that such heterogeneity is acquired prenatally, when the basal cell pool and local niches are still being established, and depends on the integrity of these niches, as supported by the altered basal cell phenotype of tracheal cartilage-deficient mouse mutants.
evidence: Data from E18.5 embryos (Figure 6) shows differential marker expression in ventral and dorsal BCs, and Sox9 mutants lacking cartilage show loss of this differential pattern.

claim: Features that distinguish progenitor subpopulations in murine airways are conserved in humans.
source: Finally, we show that features that distinguish these progenitor subpopulations in murine airways are conserved in humans.
evidence: Figure 7 shows that BC-1 and BC-2 markers are differentially expressed in ventral and dorsal human tracheal BCs.

claim: Basal cells are essential for the homeostatic maintenance and repair of the respiratory epithelium.
source: A large body of studies, over decades, has shown that BCs are essential for the homeostatic maintenance and repair of the respiratory epithelium.
evidence: This statement references established literature on basal cell function.

claim: Dysregulated airway basal cell activities by environmental exposures and repeated injuries result in aberrant self-renewal and epithelial differentiation.
source: Dysregulated airway BC activities by environmental exposures and repeated injuries are known to result in aberrant self-renewal and epithelial differentiation, often associated with chronic obstructive pulmonary diseases (COPD) and pre-neoplastic lesions that can lead to lung squamous cell carcinoma (Rock et al., 2010; Shaykhiev, 2021; Hynds and Janes, 2017; Ferone et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Basal cells differ in their ability to retain label in bromodeoxyuridine (BrdU) incorporation assays.
source: Initial clues suggesting BC heterogeneity came from studies showing that they could differ in their ability to retain label in bromodeoxyuridine (BrdU) incorporation assays, and exhibit distinct clonogenic behavior due to different ability to activate the Krt5 promoter (Borthwick et al., 2001; Schoch et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A subpopulation of Krt14+ basal cells rapidly expands to generate additional basal cells but not differentiated components of the damaged airway epithelium post-injury.
source: This hypothesis was further strengthened by the identification of a subpopulation of Krt14 +BCs, shown by lineage tracing to rapidly expand to generate additional BCs but not differentiated components of the damaged airway epithelium post-injury (Hong et al., 2004; Ghosh et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to lineage tracing studies.

claim: Airway basal cells comprise two subpopulations of multipotent stem cells that differ in their commitment from a bona fide stem cell to an intermediate luminal progenitor.
source: Long-term clonal analysis using a Krt5CreERT2 mouse line in combination with mathematical modeling, suggested that airway BCs comprise two subpopulations of multipotent stem cells. These were present in equal numbers and differed in their commitment from a bona fide stem cell to an intermediate luminal progenitor, not particularly associated with a specific cell niche (Watson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a clonal analysis study.

claim: Two discrete basal cell subpopulations can be identified immediately after severe injury of the airway epithelium, distinguished by expression of determinants of cell fate commitment to the secretory or ciliated cell lineage.
source: Mouse models of lung injury-repair have shown that, immediately after severe injury of the airway epithelium and prior to regeneration of the luminal cells, two discrete BC subpopulations can be identified and distinguished by expression of determinants of cell fate commitment to the secretory or ciliated cell lineage (Pardo-Saganta et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to an injury-repair study.

claim: Two basal cell states in the adult human lung are distinguished by the expression levels of TRP63 and NPPC.
source: One such study reports two BC states in the adult human lung, based on the degree of maturation of these cells, distinguished by the expression levels of TRP63 and NPPC (natriuretic peptide C) (Vieira Braga et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a human lung scRNA-Seq study.

claim: Human basal cells can be stratified into multipotent, proliferating, primed secretory, and activated subpopulations.
source: Another study, also in human lungs, stratifies BCs into multipotent, proliferating, primed secretory, and activated subpopulations (Carraro et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a human lung study.

claim: Human basal cells can be classified as proliferating, differentiating, or quiescent, with differential spatial enrichment in large and small airways.
source: A third study, reports human BCs as proliferating, differentiating, or quiescent, and shows differential spatial enrichment of these populations, with proliferating and differentiating BCs present only in large airways, while quiescent BCs populate both large and small airways (Travaglini et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a human lung study.

claim: Distinct basal cell phenotypes have been identified in tissues surgically dissected from the dorsal and ventral mouse trachea.
source: Using a sampling criterion based primarily on their spatial distribution, distinct BC phenotypes have been identified in tissues surgically dissected from the dorsal and ventral mouse trachea (Tadokoro et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent mouse study.

claim: Trp63CreERT2; Rosa26lox-STOP-lox-tdtomato mice show efficient tdTomato co-labeling with TRP63+KRT5+ basal cells restricted to the basal layer of the airway epithelium.
source: Co-staining of TRP63 + cells with tdTomato in tracheal sections of these mice confirmed efficient labeling of all BCs (Figure 1A–B). KRT5 overlapped with TRP63 and tdTomato, and only rare KRT5 +TRP63 and tdTom- suprabasal cells could be identified, as previously reported (Salahudeen et al., 2020; Mori et al., 2015 ; Figure 1B).
evidence: Figure 1B shows immunofluorescence images demonstrating co-labeling of tdTomato with TRP63 and KRT5.

claim: A total of 4209 single cells passed quality control in the scRNA-Seq analysis, with median values of 10,802 transcripts and 2956 genes per cell detected.
source: A total of 4209 single cells passed quality control, with median values of 10,802 transcripts and 2956 genes per cell detected (see Methods).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the scRNA-Seq data quality metrics.

claim: Six distinct basal cell subpopulations were confirmed to originate from the respiratory lineage (Epcam+Nkx2-1+) and express established adult basal cell markers (Trp63, Krt5, Aqp5, Aqp3, and Pdpn).
source: Using the Cellranger toolkit (10× Genomics), followed by marker gene annotation, we identified six distinct BC subpopulations, which were confirmed to originate from the respiratory lineage (Epcam +Nkx2-1+) and to express established adult BC markers (Trp63, Krt5, Aqp5, Aqp3, and Pdpn) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 1C shows expression of respiratory and BC markers across the identified clusters.

claim: BC-1 accounts for 46.1% of all sequenced basal cells.
source: Notably, two clusters were prominently represented, accounting for 85.8% of all sequenced BCs. They were found at an approximate 1:1 ratio and were named as BC-1 (46.1%) and BC-2 (39.7%).
evidence: This is a direct quantification from the scRNA-Seq cluster analysis.

claim: BC-2 accounts for 39.7% of all sequenced basal cells.
source: Notably, two clusters were prominently represented, accounting for 85.8% of all sequenced BCs. They were found at an approximate 1:1 ratio and were named as BC-1 (46.1%) and BC-2 (39.7%).
evidence: This is a direct quantification from the scRNA-Seq cluster analysis.

claim: BC-1 and BC-2 lack Krt14 expression while expressing comparable levels of canonical basal cell markers (Trp63, Krt5, and Krt15).
source: Both lacked Krt14 expression, while expressing comparable levels of canonical BC markers (Trp63, Krt5, and Krt15).
evidence: This is based on scRNA-Seq gene expression analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Basal-proliferating cells account for 2.1% of the total basal cell pool and are characterized by expression of Mki67, Ccna2, Aurkb, and Ube2c.
source: The remaining four clusters comprised only a small fraction of the total BC pool (14.2%). Based on their gene signatures, featuring markers associated with differentiated cell phenotypes, these were classified as Basal-proliferating (Pro.; Mki67, Ccna2, Aurkb, Ube2c: 2.1%)
evidence: This is based on scRNA-Seq cluster analysis and marker gene expression.

claim: Basal-secretory cells account for 5.8% of the total basal cell pool and are characterized by expression of Scgb1a1, Scgb3a1, Scgb3a2, and Muc5b.
source: Basal-secretory (Sec.; Scgb1a1, Scgb3a1, Scgb3a2, Muc5b: 5.8%)
evidence: This is based on scRNA-Seq cluster analysis and marker gene expression.

claim: Basal-squamous cells account for 3.3% of the total basal cell pool and are characterized by expression of Krt13, Krt4, Krt6a, and Sprr2a3.
source: Basal-squamous (Sq.; Krt13, Krt4, Krt6a, Sprr2a3: 3.3%)
evidence: This is based on scRNA-Seq cluster analysis and marker gene expression.

claim: Basal-mesenchyme-like cells account for 3.1% of the total basal cell pool.
source: and a cluster represented by expression of genes associated with mesenchymal cells (Mes.; Basal-mesenchyme-like), which accounted for 3.1% of all profiled cells
evidence: This is based on scRNA-Seq cluster analysis.

claim: BC-1 is enriched in genes associated with drug metabolism, glutathione, and retinol metabolism.
source: Gene set enrichment analysis of KEGG pathways revealed enrichment of BC-1 in genes associated with drug metabolism, glutathione, and retinol metabolism.
evidence: Figure 1E shows KEGG pathway enrichment analysis results for BC-1.

claim: BC-2 is differentially enriched in genes from the WNT, TGFb, and Hedgehog signaling pathways.
source: By contrast, BC-2 was differentially enriched in genes from the WNT, TGFb, and Hedgehog signaling pathways, as well as signatures associated with basal cell carcinoma and non-small cell lung cancer (Shin et al., 2011; Youssef et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2014; White and Lowry, 2015; Figure 1E).
evidence: Figure 1E shows KEGG pathway enrichment analysis results for BC-2, with supporting citations.

claim: TGM2 and ISL1 are enriched in KRT5+ cells of the ventral epithelium.
source: However, a more detailed analysis of these markers in longitudinal and cross sections of adult tracheas showed a remarkable enrichment of TGM2 and ISL1, markers of BC-1, in the KRT5 + cells of the ventral epithelium (Figure 2B, Figure S6).
evidence: Figure 2B shows immunofluorescence images demonstrating enrichment of TGM2 and ISL1 in ventral BCs.

claim: CD44, CAV1, and KRT17 are strongly expressed in dorsal basal cells.
source: Dorsal BCs were rather characterized by strong expression of CD44, CAV1, and KRT17, which in turn, were only weakly detected in ventral BCs (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1 show immunofluorescence images demonstrating enrichment of these markers in dorsal BCs.

claim: Quantitative analysis of fluorescence intensity confirmed significant differences in dorsal-ventral distribution of BC-1 and BC-2 markers.
source: Quantitative analysis of fluorescence intensity confirmed the significant differences in dorsal-ventral distribution of BC-1 and BC-2 markers (Figure 2C).
evidence: Figure 2C shows quantification of fluorescence intensity for BC-1 and BC-2 markers in ventral and dorsal BCs.

claim: Basal-proliferating, Basal-squamous, Basal-mesenchyme-like, and Basal-secretory cells show only isolated or rare groups of cells scattered throughout the airway epithelium with no consistent spatial distribution.
source: Interestingly, this showed only isolated or rare groups of cells scattered throughout the airway epithelium with no consistent spatial distribution, unlike the pattern seen for BC-1 and BC-2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Figure 2—figure supplement 2 shows immunofluorescence images of markers for these BC subpopulations.

claim: BC-1 and BC-2 cells isolated from adult trachea can maintain their phenotypes in vitro independent of their respective microenvironments for at least a week.
source: These observations support the hypothesis that, BC-1 and BC-2 cells isolated from the adult trachea can maintain their phenotypes in vitro, independent of their respective microenvironments for at least a week, thus providing an opportunity to assess their functional differences as adult progenitors of the airway epithelium.
evidence: Figure 3A-B shows that BC-1 and BC-2 markers maintain differential expression in cultured BCs from ventral and dorsal regions after 7 days.

claim: Organoids derived from dorsal (BC-2) cultures were found at a significantly higher number compared to those derived from ventral (BC-1) cells.
source: However, organoids derived from the dorsal (BC-2) cultures were found at a significantly higher number compared those derived from ventral (BC-1) cells (Figure 3C; 10.41 ± 0.009% vs 7.32 ± 0.006%, respectively).
evidence: Figure 3C shows quantification of organoid-forming efficiency for BC-1 and BC-2.

claim: BC-2 is enriched in key transcription factors differentially expressed and upregulated, including Krüppel-like Factors Klf4, Klf6, and Klf13, Barx2, and AP1 family members (Junb, Jund, Atf3).
source: Notably, we found key transcription factors differentially expressed and upregulated in BC-2, including the Krüppel-like Factors Klf4, Klf6, and Klf13, Barx2, and AP1 family members (Junb, Jund, Atf3) (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B), all reported to promote squamous cell commitment in stratified epithelia (Araya et al., 2007; Bialkowska et al., 2017; Sastre-Perona et al., 2019; He et al., 2015; Olson et al., 2005; Chen et al., 2018; Ding et al., 2013; Eckert et al., 2013).
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 4B shows differential expression of transcription factors in BC-2, with supporting citations.

claim: BC-2 signature is enriched in genes from the Hedgehog/TGFb/WNT pathways involved in squamous differentiation.
source: The BC-2 signature also differed in its enrichment in genes from the Hedgehog/TGFb/WNT pathways involved in squamous differentiation (Figure 1E–F, Figure 1—figure supplement 4A-B).
evidence: Figures 1E-F and Figure 1—figure supplement 4A-B show pathway enrichment in BC-2.

claim: GSEA revealed strong enrichment of a smoking-related squamous metaplasia signature in BC-2, compared to BC-1 cells.
source: Moreover, GSEA revealed strong enrichment of a smoking-related squamous metaplasia signature in BC-2, compared to BC-1 cells (Goldfarbmuren et al., 2020: Figure 1—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 4C shows GSEA results with citation to the source of the squamous metaplasia signature.

claim: Krt13, Krt4, Krt6a, and Sprr2a3 marker genes were not found in the list of the 100 most differentially-expressed genes in BC-2 compared to BC-1.
source: Importantly, none of these marker genes were found in the list of the 100 most differentially-expressed genes in BC-2 compared to BC-1, in spite of the BC-2 enrichment in regulators of the squamous cell differentiation program (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Figure 1—figure supplement 4 shows the top differentially expressed genes between BC-1 and BC-2.

claim: The shift in culture conditions from serum-based to serum-free media had a similar impact on the ability of BC-1 and BC-2 to self-renew.
source: IF and quantitative analysis of KRT5 in these organoids showed no difference in the relative number of KRT5-labeled cells between groups (BC-1: 49.43 ± 5.54%, BC-2: 58.29 ± 2.50%, p=0.17), suggesting that the shift in culture conditions (serum-based to serum-free media) had a similar impact in the ability of BC-1 and BC-2 to self-renewal.
evidence: Figure 3D-E shows quantification of KRT5+ cells in BC-1 and BC-2 organoids.

claim: The number of KRT13+ cells was significantly higher in BC-2 organoids compared to BC-1 organoids after culture condition shift.
source: By contrast, the number of KRT13 + cells was strikingly different (BC-1: 2.65 ± 1.08%, BC-2: 13.26 ± 2.86%, p=0.001) (Figure 3D–E), suggesting that the change/perturbation in the culture environment triggered a KRT13 program of differentiation in BC-2 not seen in BC-1 progenitors.
evidence: Figure 3D-E shows immunofluorescence and quantification of KRT13+ cells in organoids.

claim: BC-2 control cultures at ALI day 7 had significantly higher percentage of KRT13+ cells compared to BC-1 controls.
source: IF analysis of KRT13 + cells at ALI day 7 showed nearly no labeling in control BC-1-derived cultures in contrast to BC-2 controls, which had significantly higher percentage of KRT13 + cells (1.54 ± 0.47% and 0.39 ± 0.39% in BC-2 and BC-1, respectively), and higher levels of Krt13 expression shown by qRT-PCR (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: Figure 4A-C shows immunofluorescence and qPCR data for KRT13 in ALI cultures.

claim: BMS treatment resulted in a marked increase in number of KRT13+ cells in both BC-1 and BC-2-derived cultures.
source: BMS treatment resulted in a marked increase in number of KRT13 + cells in both BC-1 and BC-2-derived cultures.
evidence: Figure 4A-C shows immunofluorescence and quantification of KRT13+ cells in BMS-treated cultures.

claim: RA signaling disruption had a much greater impact in the induction of KRT13 in BC-2-BMS than in BC-1-BMS-derived cultures.
source: However, RA signaling disruption had a much greater impact in the induction of KRT13 in BC-2-BMS than in BC-1-BMS-derived cultures (BC-1-BMS: 5.46 ± 0.85% vs BC-2-BMS: 13.06 ± 1.72%; Figure 4A–C).
evidence: Figure 4A-C shows quantification of KRT13+ cells in BMS-treated BC-1 and BC-2 cultures.

claim: LacZ signals were clearly present in luminal cells of both ventral and dorsal epithelium but not in basal cells in RARE-LacZ reporter mice.
source: Surprisingly, LacZ signals were clearly present in luminal cells of both ventral and dorsal epithelium but not in BCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 1 shows X-gal staining and immunofluorescence in RARE-LacZ mice.

claim: Under homeostatic conditions, basal cells are unlikely to activate RA signaling.
source: This suggested that, under homeostatic conditions, BCs are unlikely to activate RA signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the RARE-LacZ reporter data showing no LacZ signal in BCs.

claim: Control (uninjured) animals showed a balanced distribution of cell phenotypes with no significant differential enrichment between dorsal and ventral cells and only rare KRT13+ cells.
source: Control (uninjured) animals (0dpi) showed a balanced distribution of these phenotypes with no significant differential enrichment between dorsal and ventral cells and only rare KRT13 + cells, also without preferential dorsal-ventral distribution (Figure 5A–C and H, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,3C-D).
evidence: Figures 5A-C, 5H, and Figure 5—figure supplements 1A and 3C-D show immunofluorescence and quantification in uninjured control tracheas.

claim: The ventral epithelium of 5dpi-Nap and 7dpi-Poli tracheas was already populated by a large number of secretory and multiciliated cells, while these profiles were still missing or greatly diminished in the dorsal side.
source: Unexpectedly, analysis of the earlier stages of regeneration in both Naphthalene and Polidocanol injury models revealed major differences in the kinetics of repopulation between the dorsal and ventral trachea. While the ventral epithelium of 5dpi-Nap and 7dpi-Poli tracheas was already populated by a large number of secretory and multiciliated cells, these profiles were still missing or greatly diminished in the dorsal side (Figure 5E and G, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-C).
evidence: Figures 5E, 5G, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-C show immunofluorescence of differentiated cell markers in injured tracheas.

claim: The dorsal epithelium showed a striking induction of KRT13 expression in KRT5+ cells and a massive increase in KRT13+ cells in the nascent regenerating luminal cells.
source: In addition, the dorsal epithelium showed a striking induction of KRT13 expression in KRT5 + cells and a massive increase in KRT13 + cells in the nascent regenerating luminal cells (Figure 5).
evidence: Figure 5 shows immunofluorescence of KRT13 in injured tracheas.

claim: In 5dpi-Nap mice, KRT13+ labeling in the tracheal epithelium increased dorsally from 0.71 ± 0.37% (control) to 45.47 ± 4.74%, while ventrally labeling increased from 0.2 ± 0.12% (control) to 8.36 ± 2.55%.
source: Indeed, in 5dpi-Nap mice KRT13 +labeling in the tracheal epithelium increased dorsally from 0.71 ± 0.37% (control) to 45.47 ± 4.74%, while ventrally labeling increased from 0.2 ± 0.12% (control) to 8.36 ± 2.55%.
evidence: This is quantification data from immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 3C.

claim: In 7dpi-Poli, KRT13+ comprised 53.41 ± 5.33% of all the dorsal regenerating epithelium, compared with only 8.69 ± 2.46% ventrally.
source: Similarly, in 7dpi-Poli KRT13 +comprised 53.41 ± 5.33% of all the dorsal regenerating epithelium, compared with only 8.69 ± 2.46% ventrally (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is quantification data from immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 3C.

claim: The differential enrichment of BC-1 and BC-2 markers in ventral and dorsal BCs, respectively, could be clearly distinguished in the epithelium undergoing regeneration in both injury models.
source: Interestingly, the differential enrichment of BC-1 and BC-2 markers in ventral and dorsal BCs, respectively, could be clearly distinguished in the epithelium undergoing regeneration in both models (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Figure 5—figure supplement 2 shows immunofluorescence of BC-1 and BC-2 markers in injured tracheas.

claim: By 15dpi, the proportion of KRT13+ labeled cells was significantly reduced in both the dorsal and ventral compartments.
source: By 15dpi when the epithelium had already extensively regenerated in both models, the proportion of KRT13 +labeled cells was significantly reduced in both the dorsal and ventral compartments (Nap: 5.79±2.19% vs 0.44 ± 0.34%; Poli:10.69±2.53% vs 0.54 ± 0.31%) (Figure S12C).
evidence: Figure 5—figure supplement 3C shows quantification of KRT13+ cells at 15dpi.

claim: Differential enrichment of BC-1 and BC-2 markers is present in pre-BCs from ventral and dorsal embryonic tracheas at E18.5.
source: Tracheas were isolated from E18.5 embryos and triple-labeled for KRT5 with each marker and a-SMA (which served as a reference for the dorsal location). This revealed significant differential enrichment of BC-1 and BC-2 markers, consistent with the pattern identified in the adult trachea.
evidence: Figure 6A shows immunofluorescence of BC-1 and BC-2 markers in E18.5 tracheas.

claim: Quantitative analysis of fluorescence intensity in E18.5 KRT5-expressing cells confirmed statistically significant difference of expression for all markers except CAV1.
source: Quantitative analysis of fluorescence intensity, specifically in KRT5-expressing cells, confirmed statistically significant difference of expression for all markers except CAV1 (Figure 6A and C).
evidence: Figure 6C shows quantification of fluorescence intensity for BC-1 and BC-2 markers in E18.5 ventral and dorsal BCs.

claim: Targeted deletion of Sox9 in the developing tracheal mesenchyme of Foxg1Cre; Sox9fl/fl mutants results in complete absence of cartilage.
source: Genetic studies have demonstrated the crucial role of Sox9 as a master regulator of cartilage cell fate (Bi et al., 1999). Targeted deletion of Sox9 in the developing tracheal mesenchyme of Foxg1Cre; Sox9fl/fl mutants results in complete absence of cartilage, a tracheal defect lethal at birth (Hines et al., 2013; Hébert and McConnell, 2000; Nasr et al., 2021; Bottasso-Arias et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to genetic studies of Sox9 function.

claim: A comparison of the intensity of signals between ventral and dorsal pre-BCs from Foxg1Cre; Sox9fl/fl mutants showed no significant difference for all markers.
source: Remarkably, a comparison of the intensity of signals between ventral and dorsal pre-BCs from mutants showed no significant difference for all markers, in sharp contrast with the findings in WT tracheas (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: Figure 6A-C shows immunofluorescence and quantification of BC-1 and BC-2 markers in E18.5 Foxg1Cre; Sox9fl/fl mutant tracheas.

claim: All but TGM2 of the five representative mouse BC-1 and BC-2 markers were expressed in human tracheal basal cells.
source: Thus, we assessed expression of the five representative mouse BC-1 and BC-2 markers in tracheal sections from adult healthy human donors. Double-labeling with KRT5 showed that all but TGM2 were expressed in BCs. Although expressed in human tracheal epithelium, TGM2 was rather present in luminal cells (Data not shown).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence analysis in human tracheal sections.

claim: Quantitation of fluorescence intensity of BC-1 and BC-2 markers revealed a pattern of differential enrichment similarly present in human ventral and dorsal BCs.
source: Quantitation of fluorescence intensity of these signals revealed a pattern of differential enrichment of mouse BC-1 and BC-2 markers similarly present in human ventral and dorsal BCs, respectively (Figure 7A).
evidence: Figure 7A shows immunofluorescence and quantification of BC-1 and BC-2 markers in human tracheal sections.

claim: Human BCs expanded to confluency showed distinctly stronger ISL1 signals in cultures isolated from ventral regions compared to dorsal BC-derived cultures.
source: IF staining of human BCs expanded to confluency showed distinctly stronger ISL1 signals in the cultures isolated from ventral (BC-1) in contrast to the dorsal BC-2-derived cultures, which were readily recognizable by the stronger CAV1, CD44, and KRT17 expression (Figure 7B).
evidence: Figure 7B shows immunofluorescence and qPCR of BC-1 and BC-2 markers in cultured human BCs.

claim: When allowed to differentiate under ALI, human dorsal BC-derived cultures consistently generated more KRT13+ cells compared to ventral BC-derived cultures.
source: Furthermore, when allowed to differentiate under ALI, human dorsal BC-derived cultures consistently generated more KRT13 + cells (Figure 7C, 45.59 ± 3.58% compared with 19.67 ± 3.98%).
evidence: Figure 7C shows immunofluorescence and quantification of KRT13+ cells in human ALI cultures.

claim: Differences between cultures from distinct human BC subpopulations could be seen even after prolonged time, as shown in ALI day 28 cells.
source: Differences between cultures from these distinct BC subpopulations could be seen even after prolonged time, as shown in ALI day 28 cells.
evidence: Figure 7C shows data from ALI day 28 human BC cultures.

claim: BC-1 and BC-2 are the most stem-like of all the BC subpopulations.
source: If present, these genes were detected at very low levels and only in few cells of the cluster. Although not enriched for specific stem cell markers, BC-1 and BC-2 appeared to be the most stem-like of all the BC subpopulations.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that BC-1 and BC-2 lack enrichment in differentiation markers compared to other BC subpopulations.

claim: BC-1 and BC-2 are the main populations responsible for epithelial regeneration in response to severe tracheal injury.
source: This further supported the idea that among all BC subtypes, BC-1 and BC-2 are the main populations responsible for epithelial regeneration in response to the severe tracheal injury.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that BC-1 and BC-2 markers are maintained during regeneration in injury models.

claim: Basal cells may produce RA or its precursors making them available to neighbor luminal cells to drive or maintain their differentiation program.
source: However, the presence of components of the RA biosynthetic pathway in BCs suggests that they may produce RA or its precursors making available to neighbor luminal cells to drive or maintain their differentiation program.
evidence: This is speculated based on the presence of RA pathway components in BCs and LacZ signals in luminal cells but not BCs in RARE-LacZ mice.

claim: BC-1 could be better equipped to produce RA compared with BC-2.
source: Interestingly, BC-1 differs from BC-2 in its enrichment in Retinol metabolism genes, suggesting that BC-1 could be better equipped of producing RA compared with BC-2.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential enrichment of retinol metabolism genes in BC-1.

claim: The extensive proliferation and expansion of KRT13+ cells seemed to occur at the costs of differentiation in dorsal BCs.
source: The extensive proliferation and expansion of KRT13 + cells seemed to occur at the costs of differentiation in dorsal BCs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that dorsal epithelium shows high KRT13 expression but low differentiated cell markers during regeneration.

claim: The induction of KRT13 in the tracheal epithelium is likely to be transient in the absence of persistent injurious stimuli.
source: This program differs from the ventral (BC-1)-associated program as it is characterized by induction of a metaplastic state associated with KRT13 expression and likely to be transient in the absence of persistent injurious stimuli.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that KRT13 expression is reduced by 15dpi when the epithelium has regenerated.

claim: Acquisition of heterogeneity is an early event that parallels BC fate specification during lung development.
source: We, thus, asked whether acquisition of heterogeneity was an early event that paralleled BC fate specification during lung development.
evidence: This is a hypothesis tested by examining BC-1 and BC-2 markers in embryonic tracheas.

claim: Local epithelial-mesenchymal crosstalks are crucial in establishing BC heterogeneity as they are being specified and undergoing maturation in the developing trachea.
source: We then reasoned that local epithelial-mesenchymal crosstalks were crucial in establishing BC heterogeneity as they were being specified and undergoing maturation in the developing trachea.
evidence: This is a hypothesis tested using Sox9 mutants lacking cartilage.

claim: Disruption of the cartilage niche could result from attenuation of local signals normally present in the ventral mesenchyme or cartilage primordia, key in creating the differences in gene expression between BC-1 and BC-2.
source: We propose this could presumably have resulted from attenuation of local signals normally present in the ventral mesenchyme or cartilage primordia, key in creating the differences in gene expression between BC-1 and BC-2.
evidence: This is speculated based on the loss of differential BC-1 and BC-2 marker expression in Sox9 mutants.

claim: Trp63 is expressed in BCs throughout the body.
source: This choice was supported by extensive evidence of Trp63 expression in BCs throughout the body and the inability of these cells to form in the absence of Trp63 (Daniely et al., 2004; Romano et al., 2012; Fletcher et al., 2011; Zhao et al., 2014; Yang et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Basal cells are unable to form in the absence of Trp63.
source: This choice was supported by extensive evidence of Trp63 expression in BCs throughout the body and the inability of these cells to form in the absence of Trp63 (Daniely et al., 2004; Romano et al., 2012; Fletcher et al., 2011; Zhao et al., 2014; Yang et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Squamous metaplasia is a reversible lesion that can lead to pre-malignant conditions.
source: In the lung, however, it is a hallmark of an aberrant program triggered by sustained epithelial injury giving rise to squamous metaplasia, a reversible lesion that can also lead to pre-malignant conditions (Araya et al., 2007; Ooi et al., 2014; Auerbach et al., 1961).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Squamous metaplasia in the respiratory epithelium is strongly linked to perturbations in the progenitor cell program triggered by disruption in the retinoic acid (RA) signaling.
source: In the respiratory epithelium, squamous metaplasia is strongly linked to perturbations in the progenitor cell program triggered by disruption in the retinoic acid (RA) signaling. This has been extensively reported as a manifestation of vitamin-A deficiency in humans and in animal models, as well as in cells cultured in the presence of pharmacological antagonists of the RA pathway (Lancillotti et al., 1992; Chopra, 1983; Choi et al., 2003; Nettesheim et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Skin basal cells (keratinocytes) metabolize retinoid precursors and serve as a source of retinol for differentiation of the upper skin layers.
source: Consistent with this, there is evidence that skin BCs (keratinocytes) metabolize retinoid precursors and serve as a source of retinol for differentiation of the upper skin layers (Kurlandsky et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Intraperitoneal injection of Naphthalene results in massive injury and sloughing of club cells of the airway epithelium.
source: Intraperitoneal injection of Naphthalene, a byproduct of the cigarette smoke metabolized by cytochrome P450 enzymes results in massive injury and sloughing of club cells of the airway epithelium.
evidence: This describes an established injury model.

claim: In the trachea, repair after Naphthalene injury is initiated by activation of a BC program of regeneration that repopulates the epithelium within 2–3 weeks.
source: In the trachea, repair is subsequently initiated by activation of a BC program of regeneration that repopulates the epithelium within 2–3 weeks (Tata et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Polidocanol induces extensive and severe epithelial sloughing when injected intratracheally in mice.
source: Polidocanol is a detergent/sclerosing agent that induces extensive and severe epithelial sloughing when injected intratracheally in mice, also eliciting a BC-mediated regenerative response that reconstitutes the airway epithelium (Paul et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a prior study.

claim: Several genes differentially enriched in the BC-2 subpopulation, such as Tppp3, Tnfrsf12a, and Cav1, have been associated with severity or aggressiveness of squamous carcinoma in various organs.
source: Interestingly, several genes found to be differentially enriched in the BC-2 subpopulation, such as Tppp3, Tnfrsf12a, and Cav1 have been associated with severity or aggressiveness of squamous carcinoma in various organs (Yang et al., 2020; Hu et al., 2019; Xue et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: A recent study identifies metaplastic variant TRP63-expressing clones in COPD patients and in fetal human lungs.
source: Additionally, a recent study identifies metaplastic variant TRP63-expressing clones in COPD patients and in fetal human lungs (Rao et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.
